main.text: It is shown that שלך salach is rightly rendered by the Greeks καταῤῥάκτην [katarrhaktēn] catarrhactes.

The Hebrew bird name שלך salach is rendered by the Greeks καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs], and quite rightly. [col. 278] For the verb השליך, from which the bird's name is derived, is the same as καταῤῥίπτειν [katarrhiptein], to throw forth, and καταβάλλειν [kataballein], to throw down. Moreover, this is the very meaning of καταῤῥάττειν [katarrhattein], from which καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs] is formed. Hesychius: Καταῤῥάσσειν· καταῤῥίπτειν [Katarrhassein· katarrhiptein]. Likewise: Καταῤῥάξαι· καταβαλεῖν [Katarrhaxai· katabalein]. Accordingly, in more than a hundred places of the Greek version the Hebrew השליך is answered by the Greek ῥίπτειν [rhiptein], ἀποῤῥίπτειν [aporrhiptein], ἐπιῤῥίπτειν [epirrhiptein], καταῤῥίπτειν [katarrhiptein], and βάλλειν [ballein], ἐκβάλλειν [ekballein], ἐμβάλλειν [emballein], ἀποβάλλειν [apoballein]. Indeed, in Psal. CI. (Hebr. CII.), for the Hebrew השליכני the Greek has κατέῤῥαξάς με [katerrhaxas me], you have thrown me down. Thus, just as καταῤῥάξαι [katarrhaxai] corresponds to the verb השליך, so καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs] corresponds to the noun שלך. And it is sometimes an epithet of birds of prey, which rush upon their prey with force and in a manner hurl themselves headlong. So Sophocles in the Laocoon had called the eagle καταῤῥάκτην [katarrhaktēn], and in the Phineus the Harpies καταῤῥάκτας [katarrhaktas]. Hesychius: Καταῤῥάκτης· ὀχετὸς, ῥύαξ, καὶ ἀετός· Σοφοκλῆς Λαοκόοντι, καὶ τὰς Ἁρπυίας ἐν Φινεῖ [Katarrhaktēs· ochetos, rhyax, kai aetos· Sophoklēs Laokoonti, kai tas Harpyias en Phinei]. And in the Cassandra of Lycophron, καταῤῥακτὴρ [katarrhaktēr], which is the same thing, is an epithet of the hawk. The words are at line 168:
Τὸν δ' αὖ τέταρτον αὐθόμαινον ὄψεται Κίρκου καταῤῥακτῆρος· — [Ton d' au tetarton authomainon opsetai / Kirkou katarrhaktēros· —]

The fourth, moreover, a kinsman, he will see, of the catarrhacter hawk, or catarrhactes. Juba also calls the Diomedean birds ^{(1)} catarrhactae, as is found in Pliny, book 10, chapter 44; because in Aristotle's Mirabilia [ch. 80] we read that they spare the Greeks but καταῤῥάσσειν [katarrhassein] the barbarians who come.

Nevertheless, just as שלך among the Hebrews, so καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs] among the Greeks is a definite species of bird, to which this name is peculiar ^{(2)}. Suidas: Καταῤῥάκτης· εἶδος ὀρνέου θαλασσίου [Katarrhaktēs· eidos orneou thalassiou].

[III, 21] σὶς [sis]: Catarractes, a species of sea bird. Eustathius on Dionysius: Τὶ ὄρνεον ἀετῶδες καταῤῥάκτης καλεῖται [ti orneon aetōdes katarrhaktēs kaleitai]: A certain bird of the eagle kind is called catarrhactes. Aristophanes in the Birds: Καὶ ἐρωδιῷ, καὶ καταῤῥάκτῃ, καὶ μελαγκορύφῳ [kai erōdiō, kai katarrhaktē, kai melankoryphō]: And to the heron, and to the catarrhactes, and to the blackcap. And there the Scholiast: Καταῤῥάκται εἰσὶ παρὰ Καλλιμάχῳ ἀναγεγραμμέναι [Katarrhaktai eisi para Kallimachō anagegrammenai]: Catarractae are described by Callimachus. Aristotle, History, book 2, chapter 17: Νῆττα δὲ, καὶ χὴν, καὶ λάρος, καὶ καταῤῥάκτης, καὶ ὠτὶς τὸν στόμαχον εὐρὺν καὶ πλατὺν ὅλον ἔχουσι [Nētta de, kai chēn, kai laros, kai katarrhaktēs, kai ōtis ton stomachon euryn kai platyn holon echousi]: The duck, the goose, the gull, the catarrhactes and the bustard have the whole stomach wide and broad. And book 9, chapter 12: Ὁ δὲ καταῤῥάκτης ζῇ μὲν περὶ θάλατταν. ὅταν δὲ καθῇ ἑαυτὸν εἰς τὸ βαθὺ, μένει χρόνον οὐκ ἐλάττονα, ἢ ὅσον πλέθρον διέλθοι τις. ἔστι δ᾽ ἔλαττον ἱέρακος τὸ ὄρνεον [Ho de katarrhaktēs zē men peri thalattan. hotan de kathē heauton eis to bathy, menei chronon ouk elattona, ē hoson plethron dielthoi tis. esti d' elatton hierakos to orneon]: The catarrhactes lives by the sea. When it has plunged into the deep, it stays there no less time than it takes a man to walk across a plethrum. The bird is smaller than a hawk. Oppian in the Ixeutica writes that it is προσόμοιον [prosomoion], similar, to the goshawk. In Eustathius it is said to be called catarrhactes ὡς ἄνωθεν καταῤῥάσσων ἐν τῷ θηρεύειν τὰ ὄρνεα [hōs anōthen katarrhassōn en tō thēreuein ta ornea], as rushing down from above when it hunts birds. Wrongly, since the catarrhactes hunts nothing but fish. It is better, therefore, to learn the reason for the name from elsewhere. And Gesner's Excerpts from Oppian's Ixeutica, which indeed no longer survive, offer themselves conveniently. He had read a manuscript Greek paraphrase of them, in which the following is most to the point [book II, ch. 2]. 1. The catarractes sits on crags, shores and rocks that stand out above the water, which they call χοιράδας [choiradas], etc. And when it has seen some fish swimming (for it is very sharp-sighted, even down to the bottom of the sea), it flies higher, and with all its feathers drawn in, as if falling into the sea, it is borne through the intervening space of air faster than any dart, and plunges to the depth of an ell, until it has seized a fish and drawn it out; then, flying up, it devours it while it is still struggling ^{(3)}. Our most learned Vossius, in that excellent work of his on Mela, page β, quotes this in Greek from his manuscripts thus: Πρὸς ὕψος ἑαυτὸν αἴρει, καὶ τὰ πτερὰ πάντα συστείλας, εἰς τὸν πόντον, [col. 279] οἷα πίπτων, οἴσεται, διατεμὼν τὸν ἀέρα, παντὸς ἂν εἴποις βέλους ὀξύτερον, καὶ καταδύεται μέχρι ὀργυιᾶς, ἢ καὶ πλέον, ἔσθ᾽ ὅτε συλλαβὼν τὸν ἰχθὺν ἀνασπᾷ, καὶ ἀνιπτάμενος ἔτι πάλλοντα κατεσθίει [Pros hypsos heauton airei, kai ta ptera panta systeilas, eis ton ponton, hoia piptōn, oisetai, diatemōn ton aera, pantos an eipois belous oxyteron, kai katadyetai mechri orgyias, ē kai pleon, esth' hote syllabōn ton ichthyn anaspa, kai aniptamenos eti pallonta katesthiei]. 2. The death of the catarrhactes is harder than that which befalls any of the birds of uncertain life. For the keenness of their eyes, dulled when they are worn out by age, causes them, thinking they are hurling themselves headlong into the sea after fish as prey, to dash against crags and cliffs and perish [III, 22] ^{(4)}. 3. Catarrhactae are caught with images of fish painted on boards. For while they rush at these as if at live fish, they dash against them and perish ^{(5)}. 4. The male carries the eggs from which he guesses a male will be produced, the female those from which a female will come, up into the air, grasped in their talons. Then they drop them into the sea, and repeat this again and again for some days. The eggs being warmed by this motion, the chicks are hatched. 5. The chicks of the catarrhacta, as soon as they have seen the light, make no delay in the nest but strive to follow their parents in flight. Taken up by the parents, they are let down into the sea and at once drawn out again, so that with the help of their parents this kind of exercise may become easier for them. You see, reader, how fittingly it is called שלך in Hebrew and καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs] in Greek. For at one point it is described as משליך נפשו, ἑαυτὸν καταῤῥάσσων [heauton katarrhassōn], casting itself down, either deliberately into the sea, from which its food is supplied, or by mistake onto crags or painted boards, whence certain destruction for it; at another as משליך ביציו או בניו, throwing its eggs or letting its chicks down into the sea. To this last, perhaps, τὸ καταῤῥάσσειν [to katarrhassein] does not so properly apply, since it is not done with violence; but the Hebrew השליך means both to let down gently and to throw with violence. It is used of throwing headlong in Ion. II, 4., where the Prophet, using this verb, complains that he had been cast into the deep, into the heart of the sea. And in 2 Par. XXV, 12., where we read of ten thousand Edomites: וישליכום, And they threw them from the top of the rock, and they were all dashed to pieces. Accordingly the Greeks render: Καὶ κατεκρήμνιζον αὐτούς [Kai katekrēmnizon autous]; and Jerome: And they cast them headlong. But it is taken for letting down when it is written of Jeremiah in Ierem. XXXVIII, 6.: וישליכו אותו אל הבור, And they cast him into the pit, that is, they let him down. For it follows by way of explanation that he was let down there with ropes. So the catarrhactes, although it does not so much throw as let down its chicks into the sea, and perhaps its eggs too, could nevertheless be called שלך for that reason as well. And I would suppose the Hebrews had caught some scent of this account when they relate, on the authority of Aben Ezra, that the שלך is a bird that is accustomed להשליך ילדיו, to throw out its young. So much for the Greek version; since it is true, it is fitting to weigh the others against it as well.

Onkelos and Jonathan here have שלינונא salenuna, and the Syriac, with the words divided, ܫܠܐ ܢܘܢܐ. In the same way some also write שלי נונא sale nuna in Jonathan, and render it plunderer of fish, as if שלי came from שלל, to plunder. But it comes from שלה, which means to draw out and to extract, like the Arabic سل [sall] and the Syriac ܫܠܐ; Psal. XVIII, 17. ושלני וקבלני מן מיא סגאה, And he drew me out, and brought [III, 23] me out of many waters. So שליכון is the extractor or drawer-out of fish. This is how R. Judah explains it in the Talmudic tractate Chullin, ch. 3, fol. 63a: שלך זה השלה דגים מן הים, Salach is the bird that draws fish out of the sea. And Kimchi on Psalm 145: מצאתי בדברי רז״ל רבי יוחנן כד הוה חזי שלך ששולה דגים הים הוא אמר משפטיך תהום רבה, I found in the writings of our masters of blessed memory that R. Johanan, when he saw the bird salach [col. 280] drawing fish out of the sea, said: Thy judgments are a great deep. The passage is Psalm 36, verse 7, by which he meant that God exercises his judgments even in the great deep, that is, in the sea. How rightly, we do not ask now. We adduce this only to show why the Syrians and Chaldeans call the שלך salach שלי נונא, that is, drawer-out of fish. It is because it is the nature of the catarrhactes not only to feed on the fish that swim in the sea, but also to draw them out from the bottom of the sea, down to a fathom deep. Hence Oppian's paraphrast above, Dionysius Characenus ^{(6)}: Καταδύεται μέχρι ὀργυιᾶς, ἢ καὶ πλέον. ἔσθ᾽ ὅτε συλλαβὼν τὸν ἰχθὺν ἀνασπᾷ [Katadyetai mechri orgyias, ē kai pleon. esth' hote syllabōn ton ichthyn anaspa], etc. And the Philosopher says that it stays at the bottom of the sea χρόνον οὐκ ἐλάττονα ἢ ὅσον πλέθρον διέλθοι τις [chronon ouk elattona ē hoson plethron dielthoi tis].

Both Arabic translators call the same bird زمج [zummaj] zummag. The name is derived from anger. زمج [zamija] zamagia is a verb meaning to be angry, and the verbal noun زمج [zamaj] zamgi means anger. So from the etymology one infers that the bird is very irascible. There are, moreover, two species. One is called simply زمج [zummaj] zummag, of which more below. The other is زمج الماء [zummaj al-māʾ] the water zummag, of which Damir says: هو طاير الذي يسمي بمصر النورس وهو ابيض في حد الحمام واكبر يعلو في الجو ثم يزج بنفسه في الما ويختلس منه السمك ولا يقع علي الجيف ولا ياكل غير السمك [huwa ṭāyir alladhī yusamī bi-Miṣr al-nawras wa-huwa abyaḍ fī ḥadd al-ḥamām wa-akbar yaʿlū fī al-jaww thumma yazujju bi-nafsihi fī al-mā wa-yakhtalisu minhu al-samak wa-lā yaqaʿu ʿalī al-jiyaf wa-lā yaʾkulu ghayr al-samak], It is the bird that in Egypt is called nauras; it is white, of the size of a dove or even larger; it flies up high, then plunges into the water to snatch fish from it; it neither descends on carcasses nor eats anything other than fish. It is evident that this fits the description of the catarrhactes ^{(7)}.

[III, 24] For catarrhactes Jerome has mergulus [little diver]. He is followed by Pagninus, Arias, Castalio, Junius, Buxtorf, the Italian and Geneva versions, and many other more recent translators. I do not approve of this, because there is no apparent reason why the diver should be called שלך, since it does not usually throw itself down from on high into the water, as the catarrhactes does. The same objection can be made to Münster and Schindler, who explain it as the heron; to Baptista Ferrarius, who has the gull, gavia, fulica; and to the English, who render it cormorant, that is, the sea raven or water raven, in Greek φαλακροκόρακα [phalakrokoraka]. And yet in the Gloss of the Talmud on the passage from the tractate Chullin cited above, it is also said to be עורב המים, the raven of the waters. But nothing is more inept than Pomarius, who renders it in Latin as mergulus with Jerome, and in Italian as מר״לו, merlo [blackbird], as if mergulus or mergus were the same as merula [blackbird].

notes.text: A species of Procellaria, perhaps procellaria puffinus Linn. Vol. 1, part 2, p. 566, ed. Gmel.; see HEYNE, Excurs. 1 ad Aen. 11, p. 580, vol. 3 of the Virgil edited by him; SCHNEIDER on Aelian 1, 1, and in the Auctarium Emendationum atque annotationum ad Aelian. at the end of the Commentarr. ad Reliqua Frider. II. p. 159. 160; BECKMANN on Aristotel. de auscultatt. mirabill. p. 157 f.

That the καταῤῥάκτης [katarrhaktēs] of the ancients is the Pelecanus Bassanus of Linnaeus, vol. 1, part 2, p. 577, ed. Gmel., with a wedge-shaped tail, white body, black bill and primary flight feathers, and blue face, was demonstrated by Oedmann in the Actis Societat. Scientiar. Holmens. [III, 21] vol. 7, 1786, p. 73—78. This paper, translated into German, was included in J. D. Michaelis' Neuer Orientalischer Bibliothek, vol. 3, no. 46, p. 65—73, and reprinted in Oedmann's Vermischten Sammlungen vol. 3, ch. 7, p. 68 ff.

This is confirmed by OLAFSEN in the Commentarii Itinerum, per Islandiam factorum, vol. 1, §. 336, p. 120. 121 of the German translation, where the pelecanus bassanus is described quite accurately. Cf. also Oedmann loc. cit. 3, p. 71.
OLAFSEN reports the same, loc. cit.
The Pelecanus Bassanus is caught today in Norway by a similar device; see PONTOPPIDAN, Naturgesch. von Norweg. vol. 2, p. 124.
The author of the Ixeutica is said by others to be Eutecnius; see the discussion of Jo. GOTTL. SCHNEIDER at the end of the Notes on book 3 of the Ixeutica, p. 437. 438 of his edition of Oppian.

Hasselquist, Itin. p. 326, reports that Abu Nures [ابو نورس] [abū nawras] is the Egyptian name of the Sterna Nilotica. That bird, he says, equals a dove in size; [III, 24] it is white on the whole abdomen, neck and throat, ash-grey on the back; its habitat is the Nile, its food small fish. All this agrees with Damiri's زمج الماء [zummaj al-māʾ] or نورس [nawras]. Oedmann, p. 73, conjectures that it is a species of gull, but does not add what arguments moved him. Yet the conjecture is not altogether unhappy: for its external appearance would suggest that it is a gull, says Hasselquist loc. cit., where he speaks of the sterna Nilot., etc.
